President Trump says he's rejecting an Iranian plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

A powerful nor'easter is slamming the northeast, prompting states to declare emergencies in
parts of New York and New Jersey, where flooding is already taking its toll.
Steve Kastenbaum reports.
With wind gusts between 40 and 60 miles per hour, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said the
impact of the storm would be felt most along the coast.
Lots of coastal flooding, perhaps even some erosion that could lead to downed trees, and

A foot or two of water covered low-lying coastal areas of New York during high tide.
The storm was pushing water up into several New Jersey shore towns.
Streets in Surf City looked more like canals.
In Delaware, the storm surge pushed an ocean buoy up into Rehoboth Beach.
The effects of this nor'easter are expected to last until Monday.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Kastenbaum in New York.
More than 31 million people are under coastal flood warnings and advisories from the Carolinas

You're listening to NPR.
It's that time of year for students and families hoping to get federal help paying for college
to fill out a form known as the FAFSA, NPR's Corey Turner reports.
It stands for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, and it's the gateway not just
to federal loans and grants, but also to a lot of state and even school-based financial
aid.
It is supposed to open on October 1st, but for the second year in a row, the Trump administration
has posted the form ahead of schedule.
In 2020, Congress moved to simplify the FAFSA, and in 2023, the Biden administration failed
to release the new and approved form on time, falling months behind schedule and sending
families and schools into a panic.
The Trump administration has made a few changes to this year's form, including making it shareable
between family members by text and getting rid of confusing jargon.
Corey Turner, NPR News.

When Sheeran returned to the stage, he made a few brief comments at the start.

I'm Lynda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.
